name: mexicanized romesco
instructions:
Spanish romesco with a light mexican lean — the classic toasted-almond + roasted-pepper + garlic + vinegar base, with ancho chili powder, raisins, and oregano as the mexican additions (each individually optional; ancho is the most important of the three). Blended into a thick dip.

Best served as a DIP with crackers or pita bread (see SERVING note — plating with baked vegetables is difficult in practice).

MAKES ~1.5 cups.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 3/4 cup almonds, TOASTED
- 1 can (~12 oz) FIRE-ROASTED BELL PEPPERS, drained (canned is best — see notes)
- 1-2 cloves raw garlic
- 2 tbsp red wine vinegar
- 1/4 cup olive oil (plus more to adjust consistency)
- 1-2 tsp tomato paste (EXTREMELY LIMITED, or skip entirely — see notes)
- salt to taste

MEXICAN ADDITIONS (each individually optional; ancho most important):
- 1-2 tsp ANCHO CHILI POWDER
- 1-2 tbsp raisins
- 1/2 tsp dried oregano

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. TOAST THE ALMONDS: dry skillet over medium-low, 3-5 min tossing frequently, until fragrant and lightly colored. Or oven at 350°F for 8-10 min. Cool slightly.

2. BLEND: add the toasted almonds, drained fire-roasted peppers, garlic, red wine vinegar, tomato paste (if using), ancho chili powder, raisins, and oregano to a food processor or blender. Pulse to a coarse paste.

3. STREAM IN OLIVE OIL: with the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil until the sauce reaches a thick, spoonable dip consistency. Not smooth — romesco wants some texture from the almonds.

4. SEASON: salt to taste. Adjust acid (more vinegar) or body (more oil) as needed.

5. SERVE: as a dip with crackers or pita bread. Keeps ~5 days in the fridge; flavors improve overnight.
notes:
Spanish romesco base with a light mexican lean. The 'mexicanized' part is three ingredients — ancho chili powder, raisins, oregano — each INDIVIDUALLY OPTIONAL. Among them ANCHO IS THE MOST IMPORTANT; if you only add one, add that. All three together is the full version; none of them gives you a plain (still valid) spanish romesco.

=== FIRE-ROASTED BELL PEPPERS — CANNED IS BEST ===

The peppers should be FIRE-ROASTED, and CANNED fire-roasted bell peppers are actually the best choice here — not a compromise. Home-roasting peppers (broiler or open flame + steam + peel) is a real production, and the canned version delivers the same smoky-sweet roasted character with zero work. The peppers are the flavor backbone of the dish, and canned fire-roasted carries that backbone fully.

=== FIRE-ROASTED TOMATOES — SKIP THEM (PEPPERS CARRY THE DISH) ===

Earlier versions of this recipe called for fire-roasted tomatoes alongside the peppers. I think they're a HASSLE and not worth it — the PEPPERS should carry most of the flavor anyway, and adding a second fire-roasted vegetable dilutes the pepper focus while adding prep/shopping overhead. The tomato slot, to the extent the dish needs one at all, is covered by the small amount of tomato paste (see below). Skip the fire-roasted tomatoes.

=== TOMATO PASTE — EXTREMELY LIMITED (1-2 TSP), OR SKIP ===

If using tomato paste at all, keep it to 1-2 TEASPOONS. The paste adds a low concentrated tomato-umami hum under the peppers — more than that and the dish starts reading tomato-forward, which fights the pepper-and-almond identity. Skipping it entirely is also fine; the dish works without.

=== ANCHO IS THE CHILE — POWDERED, AND THE OTHERS ARE GONE ===

Earlier versions listed four dried chiles (california, ancho, pasilla, guajillo). Ancho works best — the others are gone. And ANCHO CHILI POWDER (rather than whole dried chiles) is the practical form: no toasting/soaking/blending prep, and the quantity is easier to control. Ancho's raisiny-sweet mild-heat character is what bridges the spanish romesco base toward the mexican register, and it pairs directly with the actual raisins in the dish.

=== RAISINS — SWEETNESS THAT PAIRS WITH THE ANCHO ===

1-2 tbsp raisins blended in add a background sweetness that rounds the vinegar and echoes ancho's raisiny character. Optional but good. (Spanish romesco tradition doesn't have them; this is part of the mexicanized lean.)

=== TOASTED ALMONDS — SAME RULE AS EVERYWHERE ===

Toast the almonds first. Raw almonds read flat; toasted almonds bring the roasty depth that anchors the sauce. Same principle as toasted walnuts in [[lentil-wellington]] / [[bolognese]] variant B.

=== RAW GARLIC — KEEP THE BITE ===

The garlic goes in raw (spanish tradition) — its sharpness balances the sweet peppers and raisins. 1-2 cloves; err toward 1 if your cloves are large or you're sensitive to raw garlic heat.

=== NO BREAD ===

CLASSIC ROMESCO USES FRIED BREAD for body; this version skips it — the almonds alone carry the body, and skipping bread keeps the dish simpler (and gluten-free incidentally).

=== PORCINI POWDER (SECONDARY) — A SMOKINESS CORRECTOR, NOT AN UMAMI ADD ===

Porcini mushroom powder is a SECONDARY tool here with a specific rescue job: if you've OVERDONE THE TOMATO (or other ingredients) and the dish has drifted away from its smoky-pepper register, a small amount of porcini powder pushes the SMOKINESS and MEXICAN-NESS back up. It's not there to increase umami — the pepper + almond + ancho stack doesn't need an umami layer — it's there as a register-corrector when the balance slips. Don't reach for it by default; reach for it when the dish tastes too tomato-forward or too flat-sweet and needs the smoky-dark direction reinforced.

=== SERVING — DIP WITH CRACKERS OR PITA (NOT PLATED WITH VEGETABLES) ===

Best served as a DIP with crackers or pita bread. I've found plating it with baked vegetables (the composed-plate presentation — romesco under roasted cauliflower or asparagus) to be VERY DIFFICULT in practice — the sauce-to-vegetable proportions are hard to get right on the plate and the presentation fights you. The dip format sidesteps all of that and is how this actually gets eaten.
